description: We are three engineering students from Argentina who love space, maps and problem-solving. Our skills span software development, data engineering, geospatial analysis and machine learning. In one weekend we built RedWays, a tool that turns NASA Mars data into safe, science-driven Marswalk plans. We care about turning open data into clear decisions, and we enjoy learning fast as a team. If you like Mars, code or data, we'd love to collaborate!
summary:
RedWays is a web-based mission planner that helps a human explorer prepare and carry out a safe, science-driven Marswalk in Gale Crater. It shows a real section of Gale in interactive 3D (CesiumJS with Cesium Mars). Users pick a science goal, a destination and their tasks, then set up their walk on foot or with a support robot.

Our routing engine runs on a 1-meter HiRISE elevation model (MRO). It treats climbing and descending as different costs and finds the path out and back. It checks the whole trip against the time budget, a safety reserve, and the real sunset time measured by Curiosity’s REMS station (MSL). Each plan is labeled viable, conditional or incompatible, with the reasons. A simulated tracking mode replays the walk, adds a delay and re-evaluates whether to continue or head back. Machine-learning models trained on past REMS and RAD data add pressure, temperature and radiation context.

Every layer and rule shows its source mission, instrument and product. This turns scattered orbital and surface data into decisions an astronaut can trust: where to go, how to get there, and when to come back.
details:
What it does and how it works

RedWays is a web app for planning a Marswalk on a real part of Gale Crater, the area Curiosity is exploring. The planner opens a 3D view of the terrain and picks a mission type: geological observation, topographic survey, reconnaissance or environmental measurement. Then they choose a destination, the tasks to do there and how long each takes, and the team: one to four astronauts, plus up to two support robots if they want them.

A Python engine builds a directed 8-neighbor graph from a 1-meter HiRISE elevation model and runs Dijkstra on it twice: once for the way out and once, on the reversed graph, for the way back. Going uphill and downhill cost different amounts, and no team member is sent over terrain beyond their limits. The group moves at the pace of its slowest member, and the result says who sets the limit. The engine adds up the walk out, the tasks, the walk back and a safety reserve, and compares the total with the time budget and the sunset for that sol at that location. Each plan comes back as viable, conditional, incompatible or not enough evidence, with the reasons.

Routes are compared on three criteria, one of them the time spent without confirmed line of sight to the base. Each route card shows its estimated line of sight to the base: time visible, time hidden and the longest stretch without visibility. A simulated tracking mode moves the team along the path, adds a delay and asks the engine whether to continue or turn back. The time already spent is counted, so the limits never reset.

Benefits and intended impact

Today the data needed to plan a walk is scattered across missions, instruments and formats. RedWays brings it into one decision: where to go, which way, and when to come back. Every layer and rule has an info button that shows its mission, instrument, product, date, and whether it was live or cached. It also says whether the data was measured, derived, modeled or assumed. We want astronauts and mission planners to trust the plan because they can check where each part of it comes from.

Data and tools

NASA data: MRO/HiRISE (terrain), MSL/REMS (weather and sunrise/sunset), MSL/RAD (radiation dose), MSL traverse data (rover positions), plus NASA DONKI and MAVEN for space weather. Cesium Mars basemap built from MGS/MOLA, Mars Express/HRSC and Viking.
Frontend: TypeScript, Vite, CesiumJS with Cesium Mars.
Backend: Python, NumPy, SciPy (sparse-graph Dijkstra), rasterio/GDAL for Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs and viewshed, and a local HTTP service that caches every source.

Machine learning: LightGBM and ridge models trained on past REMS and RAD data forecast pressure, temperature and radiation dose a few sols ahead, with uncertainty ranges. On a held-out test window, the pressure forecast had about 70% less error than seasonal climatology. The forecasts appear in the app as context; they don’t change whether a mission is approved.
Development: Git/GitHub, ChatGPT and Claude as coding and research assistants.

What makes it creative


RedWays doesn’t just stack map layers: each kind of data changes a decision. Terrain sets the route, REMS sunset sets the deadline, and line of sight shapes communication risk. The tool plans the full round trip, not just the way there, and replans during the walk. It also says honestly when the data isn’t enough to decide, including when our own forecasts don’t beat simple baselines.

Factors we considered

Astronaut safety came first: return margin, a reserve, daylight and line of sight to the base. We also considered how suits and support robots affect mobility, and that a team is only as fast as its slowest member. On the data side, we kept to resolution limits (a 1 m grid can’t see every rock) and kept measured data separate from models and assumptions. We used no vertical exaggeration and no invented success percentages. For the live demo, we planned for APIs going down by falling back to cached copies.
